GENDER
 
IN
 
HUMANITARIAN
 
ACTION
 
WORKING
 
GROUP
 
UKRAINE 
 
 
 
 
Gender in Humanitarian Action Working Group Meeting Minutes Time: 14:00 - 15:30 Date: June 03, 2025 Venue: online & 9B Mykhailo Hrushevsky Street, Parkova Doroga, Kyiv, 01021, 
Ukraine
 Agenda: 1. Results of the Monitoring of Women’s Rights (2022–2025) by the National 
Network
 
Women’s
 
Consortium
 
of
 
Ukraine
 2. Key insights from the global Women Deliver conference in Naarm (Melbourne) 3. Documenting and Investigating Crimes Against LGBTIQ+ Individuals in 
Situations
 
of
 
Armed
 
Conflict
 
by
 
NGO
 
PROJECTOR
 All presentations and material are available at the link: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/17me8FppufAKLPOEfclhPa9Zp76QkfHqW 1. Results of the Monitoring of Women’s Rights (2022–2025) by the National 
Network
 
Women’s
 
Consortium
 
of
 
Ukraine,
 
Larysa
 
Magdyuk
 Larysa Magdyuk presented the findings outlined in the analytical report on the monitoring of 
women’s
 
rights
 
for
 
2022–2025.
 
During
 
the
 
monitoring
 
process,
 
more
 
than
 
50
 
female
 
respondents
 
participated
 
in
 
surveys
 
and
 
focus
 
groups.
 
The
 
key
 
objective
 
of
 
the
 
monitoring
 
was
 
to
 
assess
 
how
 
Ukraine’s
 
obligations
 
under
 
the
 
CEDAW
 
Convention
 
are
 
being
 
fulfilled
 
during
 
the
 
war.
 
Nine
 
articles
 
of
 
the
 
Convention
 
were
 
selected
 
for
 
monitoring.
 
The
 
main
 
point
 
highlighted
 
in
 
the
 
report
 
is
 
that
 
women’s
 
rights
 
cannot
 
be
 
viewed
 
in
 
isolation
 
from
 
the
 
broader
 
context
 
of
 
the
 
challenges
 
associated
 
with
 
the
 
war
 
in
 
Ukraine.
 The first set of challenges identified by the monitoring concerns the care crisis. Women 
continue
 
to
 
bear
 
the
 
primary
 
burden
 
of
 
caring
 
for
 
their
 
families,
 
children,
 
elderly
 
relatives,
 
veterans,
 
and
 
the
 
wounded.
 
As
 
a
 
result,
 
many
 
of
 
them
 
are
 
excluded
 
from
 
the
 
labor
 
market.
 
The
 
second
 
set
 
of
 
challenges
 
is
 
unequal
 
access
 
to
 
services.
 
In
 
many
 
regions
 
of
 
Ukraine,
access to services - especially medical services - and infrastructure is limited. ID women 
often
 
remain
 
isolated
 
in
 
the
 
communities
 
to
 
which
 
they
 
have
 
moved,
 
despite
 
the
 
existence
 
of
 
support
 
programs.
 
The
 
third
 
set
 
of
 
challenges
 
is
 
economic
 
isolation
 
or
 
even
 
exclusion.
 
These
 
are
 
circumstances
 
that
 
force
 
women
 
to
 
take
 
lower-paying
 
jobs
 
that
 
may
 
not
 
even
 
be
 
related
 
to
 
their
 
education
 
or
 
previous
 
experience.
 
The
 
fourth
 
set
 
of
 
challenges
 
is
 
invisible
 
vulnerability.
 
These
 
are
 
cases
 
of
 
domestic
 
and
 
GBV
 
that
 
often
 
remain
 
unseen.
 
 The first area addressed in the analytical report is the realization of women’s rights in 
political
 
life.
 
The
 
report
 
notes
 
the
 
purely
 
formal
 
nature
 
of
 
gender
 
quotas,
 
the
 
inability
 
of
 
women
 
to
 
participate
 
in
 
the
 
country’s
 
political
 
life
 
due
 
to
 
their
 
experiences
 
of
 
displacement,
 
the
 
insufficient
 
participation
 
of
 
female
 
military
 
personnel,
 
and
 
barriers
 
related
 
to
 
discrimination.
 
The
 
next
 
area
 
is
 
civic
 
activism,
 
where
 
women
 
were
 
the
 
most
 
active
 
volunteers
 
at
 
the
 
start
 
of
 
the
 
full-scale
 
war.
 
However,
 
as
 
government
 
and
 
tax
 
controls
 
increased,
 
the
 
level
 
of
 
volunteering
 
declined.
 
Legislation
 
on
 
volunteering
 
is
 
not
 
geared
 
toward
 
supporting
 
women’s
 
volunteering.
 
The
 
instability
 
of
 
funding
 
for
 
women’s
 
organizations
 
and
 
the
 
overburdening
 
of
 
women
 
also
 
pose
 
challenges.
 
A
 
new
 
issue
 
that
 
has
 
emerged
 
is
 
physical
 
and
 
emotional
 
exhaustion.
 
In
 
the
 
field
 
of
 
education,
 
the
 
main
 
challenge
 
is
 
online
 
education
 
and
 
learning
 
losses.
 
In
 
the
 
health
 
sector,
 
the
 
biggest
 
challenge
 
is
 
the
 
lack
 
of
 
information
 
for
 
women
 
about
 
their
 
medical
 
rights
 
and
 
options,
 
as
 
well
 
as
 
the
 
lack
 
of
 
systematic
 
attention
 
to
 
women’s
 
mental
 
health
 
issues.
 
In
 
the
 
socio-economic
 
sphere,
 
the
 
problem
 
is
 
a
 
lack
 
of
 
jobs
 
and
 
resulting
 
long-term
 
unemployment
 
among
 
women,
 
particularly
 
for
 
IDPs,
 
as
 
well
 
as
 
insufficient
 
opportunities
 
for
 
retraining
 
and
 
flexible
 
employment.
 Another section of the report addresses temporary special measures and protection during 
maternity.
 
Damage
 
to
 
medical
 
infrastructure
 
is
 
affecting
 
women’s
 
access
 
to
 
health
 
care
 
services.
 
A
 
new
 
and
 
significant
 
issue
 
is
 
the
 
lack
 
of
 
legal
 
options
 
for
 
civil
 
partnerships.
 The issue of human trafficking receives special attention in the monitoring. Due to the war, 
migration,
 
and
 
economic
 
vulnerability,
 
the
 
risk
 
of
 
human
 
trafficking
 
for
 
women
 
and
 
children
 
is
 
increasing.
 Regarding issues related to gender-based violence against women, there are gaps in 
legislation,
 
and
 
insufficient
 
coordination
 
among
 
all
 
responders
 
and
 
available
 
specialists.
 
There
 
is
 
stigma
 
and
 
mistrust
 
of
 
institutions
 
on
 
the
 
part
 
of
 
victims.
 
Society
 
exhibits
 
tolerance
 
toward
 
GBV
 
and
 
discrimination.
 
The
 
number
 
of
 
cyberviolence
 
cases
 
is
 
rising,
 
and
 
there
 
is
 
a
 
lack
 
of
 
response
 
mechanisms.
 
 2. Key Takeaways from the Women Deliver Global Conference in Naarm (Melbourne), 
Milena
 
Goryachkovska
 Milena Goryachkovska shared her experience of attending the Women Deliver conference. The conference brings together up to 12,000 participants from around the world and has a 
less
 
formal
 
atmosphere.
 
It
 
tends
 
to
 
address
 
the
 
pressing
 
issues
 
highlighted
 
by
 
the
 
women’s
 
movement.
 
This
 
year,
 
there
 
were
 
6,000
 
participants,
 
3%
 
of
 
whom
 
were
 
from
 
Europe.
 
There
 
were
 
three
 
representatives
 
from
 
Ukraine.
 
A
 
major
 
focus
 
of
 
this
 
year’s
 
conference
 
was
 
on
 
the
rights of indigenous peoples, decolonization, and climate justice with an intersectional 
approach.
 
 Feminist approaches to the use of artificial intelligence were also discussed at the conference. Somewhat less attention was paid to the topics of women’s economic empowerment, 
combating
 
gender-based
 
violence,
 
and
 
the
 
rights
 
of
 
women
 
with
 
disabilities.
 There was almost no coverage of Agenda 1325 Women, Peace, and Security or the UN 
Security
 
Council,
 
which
 
is
 
very
 
different
 
from
 
the
 
discussions
 
taking
 
place
 
in
 
Ukraine.
 
According
 
to
 
Milena’s
 
observations,
 
the
 
international
 
community
 
is
 
aware
 
of
 
events
 
in
 
Ukraine,
 
but
 
they
 
remain
 
on
 
the
 
periphery
 
of
 
the
 
discourse.
 
Much
 
more
 
attention
 
was
 
paid
 
to
 
events
 
in
 
Gaza.
 
In
 
addition,
 
other
 
wars
 
were
 
also
 
discussed.
 At this conference, the so-called Melbourne Declaration on Gender Equality was approved. It 
is
 
a
 
visionary
 
document
 
preceded
 
by
 
lengthy
 
interregional
 
consultations.
 
 Milena shared some links that might be useful in the context of our discussion about the 
Conference:
 ● Declaration on Gender Equality https://womendeliver.org/wd2026/melbourne-declaration-for-gender-equality/ ● The Issue of Adolescent Girls https://womendeliver.org/the-adolescent-girls-era/ ● Manifesto of Adolescent Girls https://womendeliver.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Girls-Deliver-Manifesto-En-041326.pdf ● Statement by Indigenous Women https://womendeliver.org/publications/first-nations-indigenous-women-statement/ ● Charter for a Feminist Health System https://womendeliver.org/publications/feminist-health-systems-charter/ 3. Documenting and Investigating Crimes Against LGBTIQ+ Individuals in Situations 
of
 
Armed
 
Conflict
 
by
 
NGO
 
PROJECTOR,
 
Vitalii
 
Matvieiev
 Vitaliy Matveev shared insights into the work of the NGO PROJECTOR in documenting and 
investigating
 
war
 
crimes
 
against
 
LGBTQI+
 
individuals.
 
The
 
organization
 
has
 
recorded
 
over
 
250
 
cases
 
in
 
which
 
members
 
of
 
the
 
LGBTQI+
 
community
 
have
 
served
 
as
 
witnesses,
 
eyewitnesses,
 
or
 
victims
 
since
 
2023.
 
The
 
community
 
faces
 
war
 
crimes
 
directly
 
linked
 
to
 
SOGI
 
or
 
people’s
 
physical
 
appearance
 
or
 
representation
 
in
 
society.
 
Russian
 
military
 
personnel
 
single
 
out
 
such
 
individuals
 
and
 
subject
 
them
 
to
 
additional
 
criminal
 
acts.
 
 The community rarely turns to the Ukrainian law enforcement system because there were 
already
 
issues
 
with
 
the
 
system’s
 
response
 
to
 
reports
 
even
 
before
 
the
 
full-scale
 
invasion.
 
Since
 
reports
 
from
 
the
 
LGBTQI+
 
community
 
were
 
not
 
singled
 
out
 
in
 
any
 
way,
 
it
 
is
 
impossible
 
to
 
collect
 
statistical
 
data
 
on
 
their
 
number
 
or
 
the
 
number
 
of
 
victims.
 
The
 
number
 
of
 
cases
 
of
 
war
 
crimes
 
has
 
increased
 
significantly.
 
To
 
date,
 
there
 
are
 
only
 
9
 
officially
 
recognized
 
cases.
 
These
are 9 people who agreed to speak publicly about having been victims of war crimes 
committed
 
by
 
Russian
 
military
 
personnel.
 
 The NGO PROJECTOR has developed a guide containing recommendations on the specific 
aspects
 
of
 
investigating
 
crimes
 
against
 
LGBTQI+
 
individuals
 
in
 
situations
 
of
 
armed
 
conflict.
 
 Action points: 1. Read the report on the results of the monitoring of women's rights 2. Share information about the UWF travel grant competition for women activists and take advantage of this opportunity if needed 3. Use the guide from the NGO PROJECTOR and share information about it and the app for victims developed by the organization

Article 5 / A Member of the United Nations against which preventive or enforcement action has been taken by the Security Council may be suspended from the exercise of the rights and privileges of mem- bership by the General Assembly upon the recom- mendation of the Security Council.

Article 6 A Member of the United Nations which has persistently violated the Principles contained in the present Charter may be expelled from the Organization by the General Assembly upon the recommendation of the Security Council.

Accordingly, our respective Governments, through representatives assembled in the city of San Francisco, who have exhibited their full powers found to be in good and due form, have agreed to the present Charter of the United Nations and do hereby establish an international organization to be known as the United Nations.

related.excerpt: As delivered Thank you, Mr. President, and I thank the Special Envoy [for the Secretary-General for Yemen, Hans Grundberg] for his efforts to secure a political settlement in Yemen and echo both his wishes and his hopes that the US-Iran ceasefire can bring much needed respite to the region. Congratulations on the detainee release mediation. Mr. President, colleagues, Yemen’s humanitarian crisis is accelerating. Hunger is rising. Our response is stretched to the limit. In just one month, the share of people unable to meet basic food needs jumped from half to nearly 60 per cent. Those facing the most extreme deprivation rose from one in four to nearly one in three. And today, more than 18 million people – over half the population – are acutely hungry. Without urgent action, this will worsen. In Government-controlled areas, nearly half the population – around 5 million people – face severe hunger. More than a quarter are in emergency conditions. In Houthi-controlled areas, we lack access – and therefore visibility. But a lack of data does not mean a lack of need. Yemenis may be out of sight. They must not be out of mind.
